1	# Idea Brief: Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction: When Execution Semantics Help Code Behavior Classification but Not Generation
2	
3	
4	- **Idea ID**: `idea_009`
5	- **Created**: 2026-05-14
6	- **Approved**: 2026-05-14
7	- **Source**: foreign:be-idea-gen-0509-5
8	- **Level**: top-tier
9	- **Target Venues**: EMNLP 2026 (ARR submission deadline: May 25, 2026; commitment deadline: August 2, 2026; conference: October 24–29, 2026, Budapest)
10	
11	## Seed Topic
12	
13	Target: EMNLP 2026, ARR submission deadline 2026-05-25 (16 days from today 2026-05-09). Track: NLP and Code Models.
14	
15	Direction: Code understanding and generation — repo-level comprehension, program repair, code reasoning, debugging, test generation, code-to-documentation, cross-language code transfer. NOT just code completion — focus on higher-level code reasoning tasks.
16	
17	Contribution type: METHOD ONLY. Propose new training methods, retrieval-augmented code repair, or inference algorithms for code tasks. Not a new benchmark or leaderboard entry.
18	
19	HARD CONSTRAINTS:
20	1. Compute: ≤200 H100-hours total. Code models are often evaluated zero-shot or few-shot — budget goes to SFT/LoRA if fine-tuning.
21	2. Time: ≤16 days. Build on existing code models (DeepSeek-Coder-V2, StarCoder2, CodeLlama, Qwen2.5-Coder) and frameworks (aider, SWE-agent, Moatless).
22	3. Eval: SWE-bench Verified, HumanEval/MBPP, CrossCodeEval, RepoBench, DebugBench, CodeContests.
23	
24	Look for: repo-level context compression for code understanding, retrieval-augmented repair with semantic code search, code reasoning via execution feedback, cross-repo transfer learning. Avoid: simple prompt templates for code completion.
25	
26	Tag: direction=code_models, contribution_type=method. target_venues=["EMNLP 2026 Main", "EMNLP 2026 Findings"].
27	
28	## Generation Journey
29	
30	1. **Start** — 开始生成，seed: 'Target: EMNLP 2026, ARR submission deadline 2026-05-25 (16 days from today 2026-05-09). Track: Machine Learning for NLP / Resources and Evaluation. Aligns with EMNLP 2026 special theme "New Missions for NLP Research" which explicitly calls for work on data contamination, synthetic data feedback loops, and data governance.\n\nDirection: Synthetic data quality, model collapse prevention, contamination detection. In-scope: synthetic data verification/filtering methods, detecting training data contamination in benchmarks, methods to break recursive data feedback loops, data mixing strategies that prevent quality degradation, principled synthetic data generation with quality guarantees.\n\nContribution type: METHOD ONLY. Must propose a concrete detection algorithm, filtering pipeline, or training recipe — not just an observation about model collapse. Method + analysis OK.\n\nHARD CONSTRAINTS:\n1. Compute: ≤200 H100-hours total. Model collapse experiments need multiple training iterations — budget for small models (1B-3B) across 3-5 generations.\n2. Time: ≤16 days. Use small open models (Pythia, OLMo-1B, Qwen-0.5B/1.8B) for iterative collapse experiments.\n3. Eval: perplexity degradation curves, downstream task quality (MMLU, HellaSwag), diversity metrics (self-BLEU, n-gram entropy), contamination detection accuracy.\n\nThis is a hot EMNLP 2026 special theme area with relatively few established methods — high novelty potential.\n\nTag: direction=data_governance, contribution_type=method. target_venues=["EMNLP 2026 Main", "EMNLP 2026 Findings"].'
31	2. **Problem Discovery** (325s) — 发现 4 个研究方向
32	   - Training-Time Early Warning Signals for Model Collapse
33	   - Generational Depth Fingerprinting for Synthetic Text Triage
34	   - Diversity-Calibrated Verification for Collapse-Resistant Synthetic Data
35	   - Collapse-Aware Adaptive Mixing for Synthetic-Real Training
36	3. **Method Synthesis** (287s) — 完成: "Training-Time Early Warning Signals for Model Collapse" [top-tier] → EMNLP 2026 (ARR submission May 25, 2026 — special theme: Data as a Bottleneck and a Responsibility), AAAI 2027 (expected deadline ~August 2026)
37	3. **Method Synthesis** (779s) — 完成: "Generational Depth Fingerprinting for Synthetic Text Triage" [solid] → EMNLP 2026 (ARR deadline: May 25, 2026), AAAI 2027 (paper deadline: August 2, 2026), ICLR 2027 (paper deadline: September 24, 2026), NAACL 2027 (ARR deadline: October 16, 2026), EACL 2027 (ARR deadline: October 16, 2026)
38	3. **Method Synthesis** (557s) — 完成: "Diversity-Calibrated Verification for Collapse-Resistant Synthetic Data" [solid] → EMNLP 2026 (ARR deadline: May 25, 2026), AACL-IJCNLP 2026 (ARR deadline: May 25, 2026), AAAI 2027 (abstract: July 25, 2026; paper: August 1, 2026)
39	3. **Method Synthesis** (616s) — 完成: "Collapse-Aware Adaptive Mixing for Synthetic-Real Training" [solid] → EMNLP 2026 (ARR submission deadline: May 25, 2026), AAAI 2027 (paper deadline: August 1, 2026), NeurIPS 2026 Workshops (suggested submission: August 29, 2026), ICLR 2027 (estimated deadline: September-October 2026, not yet announced)
40	
41	## Core Problem
42	
43	"Do Code Semantics Help?" (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.11686) concluded that execution trace-based SFT provides limited benefit for Code LLMs, finding it fails to improve code synthesis in 7/9 configurations and yields inconsistent results for CRUXEval reasoning tasks. TracePile (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2510.23629) scaled trace SFT to 2.6M samples across four base models and 20 benchmarks, achieving strong gains on math and code reasoning — but evaluated only generative tasks. Across all existing trace SFT studies, every task requires generating exact outputs: complete programs, precise I/O values, repaired code, or mathematical derivations. We ask: does trace SFT help for code behavior verdict tasks — binary/categorical predictions about execution outcomes (pass/fail, correct/incorrect, buggy/clean) — where the output space is fundamentally constrained? Moreover, can a trace representation specifically designed for classification (capturing only decision-relevant execution states) outperform trace formats designed for full execution simulation? This distinction — verdict prediction with task-optimized trace representation vs. open generation with simulation-oriented traces — has not been systematically investigated.
44	
45	## Opportunity / Why Now
46	
47	Four converging lines of evidence suggest trace SFT may differentially benefit verdict tasks over generation, and that a task-optimized trace representation can amplify this benefit. First, SemCoder (NeurIPS 2024) demonstrates that trace-supervised training teaches genuine behavioral understanding (63.6% CRUXEval-I vs. 50.3% for Code Llama 34B). Second, TracePile (NeurIPS 2025) shows that even at 2.6M-sample scale, trace SFT has only been applied to generative tasks — the classification regime is entirely untested. Third, TRACED (ICSE 2024) provides a precedent from the pre-training paradigm: execution-aware pre-training significantly improves encoder-model performance on classification tasks (vulnerability detection, clone retrieval), suggesting that execution understanding transfers to classification — but nobody has tested this for decoder SFT. Fourth, "Debugging Code World Models" (arXiv 2602.07672) identifies token-budget exhaustion as a dominant failure mode in dense trace representations, motivating our design of a compact, verdict-focused trace format.
48	
49	The practical stakes are high: automated patch correctness assessment (APCA) plateaus at ~88% accuracy (ComPass: 88.35%, Historian: 88.4%) using purely static features, test outcome prediction is increasingly critical for efficient CI/CD, and bug detection accuracy determines triage quality. An ensemble combining trace-SFT behavioral analysis with static approaches could break the 90% APCA barrier — a concrete practical headline. The study design ensures publishable value regardless of outcome: if our Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction (VOTA) helps for verdict tasks, we contribute both a novel trace representation and a new task regime where code semantics help; if it doesn't, we strengthen and extend the DCSH negative finding with quantitative calibration analysis explaining WHY traces fail across the full task spectrum.
50	
51	## Landscape (SOTA & Limitations)
52	
53	Trace SFT for Code LLMs: "Do Code Semantics Help?" (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.11686) is the central prior work. Testing five trace representations (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise) across DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, and Gemma2-9B, they found trace SFT fails for code synthesis (7/9 configs), yields marginal gains for program repair (+0.3–1.4 pts with SemCoder only), and shows inconsistent CRUXEval results. Crucially, all their tasks are generative — no verdict/classification tasks were evaluated, and their trace representations were designed for execution simulation, not classification. TracePile (arXiv 2510.23629, NeurIPS 2025) represents the largest-scale trace SFT effort: 2.6M Chain of Execution (CoE) samples across LLaMA 3, LLaMA 3.1, Qwen-2.5, and Qwen-2.5 Coder, evaluated on 20 benchmarks covering math, code, logic, and algorithms. It achieves strong gains (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B CRUXEval: 23.5% → 49.4%) but exclusively targets generative tasks — verdict/classification tasks are absent from their evaluation, reinforcing our gap. SemCoder (arXiv 2406.01006, NeurIPS 2024) trains on monologue-style NL execution descriptions and achieves strong CRUXEval gains, showing trace training CAN teach behavioral understanding. Execution Tuning (E.T., arXiv 2503.05703, 2025) achieves ~80% on CRUXEval-O with dynamic scratchpads but requires traces at inference time — we aim to internalize this capability via SFT. ExecVerify (arXiv 2603.11226, 2026) uses white-box RL rewards from execution traces, enabling 7B ≈ 32B on reasoning benchmarks. "Code Execution as Grounded Supervision" (arXiv 2506.10343, EMNLP 2025) extracts verifiable CoT from code execution for general reasoning. Self-Execution Simulation (arXiv 2604.03253, 2026) trains on NL traces + RL for competitive programming self-verification (+5.5% via best-of-k).
54	
55	Execution Traces for Code Classification (Pre-training Paradigm): TRACED (arXiv 2306.07487, ICSE 2024) is an important precedent: it pre-trains code language models with source code, executable inputs, and execution traces, then fine-tunes on downstream classification tasks including vulnerability detection and clone retrieval, significantly outperforming statically pre-trained models. This demonstrates that execution understanding transfers to classification. However, TRACED uses encoder-based pre-training (not decoder SFT), operates at the pre-training stage (not task-specific SFT), and does not test on verdict tasks (pass/fail, patch correctness). Our work extends this insight to the decoder SFT paradigm and tests it systematically on code behavior verdict tasks.
56	
57	Correctness Signals in Code SFT: FGIT (arXiv 2503.16913, ASE 2025) uses correct/incorrect code signal during SFT with dynamic loss weighting on error-sensitive segments, achieving 6.9% relative improvement on pass@1 for code generation. While technically different (loss reweighting for generation, not trace-supervised classification), it occupies a conceptually adjacent space: leveraging fault information to improve code SFT. Our approach differs in both objective (classification vs. generation) and mechanism (trace-grounded reasoning vs. loss reweighting).
58	
59	Automated Patch Correctness Assessment (APCA): ComPass (arXiv 2602.07561, 2026) achieves 88.35% accuracy on Defects4J via contrastive learning on BERT representations — purely static. Historian (arXiv 2603.00649, 2026) achieves 88.4% accuracy with 95.0% coverage by comparing patches against historically validated fixes — also static. APSG/Graph-LoRA (arXiv 2505.02629, 2025) reaches 85.8–96.8% via attributed semantic graphs + LLaMA3 fine-tuning. RePaCA (arXiv 2507.22580, 2025) uses reasoning LLMs with generic CoT at 83.1%. LLM4PatchCorrect (TSE 2024) is the closest existing work: it uses execution traces as in-context learning input for StarCoder, achieving 84.4% accuracy — but requires traces at inference time (expensive), while we internalize trace reasoning via SFT. Shibboleth (ISSTA 2022) achieves 88.7% but requires test execution at inference. APPT (TSE 2024) uses BERT+LSTM at 79.7%. No existing APCA method uses trace-supervised SFT with a verdict-optimized trace representation.
60	
61	Calibration of Code LLMs: Spiess et al. (arXiv 2402.02047, ICSE 2025) establish the first calibration framework for code-generating models, finding they are poorly calibrated out-of-the-box and that Platt scaling helps. However, they study calibration only for generation tasks. "Do Code Semantics Help?" (Table 7) observed that trace SFT boosts prediction confidence without increasing correctness for generative tasks. We hypothesize this overconfidence effect is beneficial for classification (sharper decision boundaries) while harmful for generation (confidently wrong outputs), and we operationalize this with ECE, Brier score, and reliability diagrams — the first quantitative calibration analysis of trace SFT across the verdict-generation spectrum.
62	
63	Benchmarks: CRUXEval (arXiv 2401.03065, ICML 2024) provides 800 Python functions for execution prediction. LiveCodeBench (arXiv 2403.07974) offers contamination-free code evaluation. DebugBench (2024) has 4,253 instances across C++/Java/Python with 18 bug types. CrossCodeEval (arXiv 2310.11248, NeurIPS 2023) evaluates cross-file code completion across 4 languages. RepoBench (arXiv 2306.03091, ICLR 2024) evaluates repository-level code completion; we exclude it because (a) it is a generation benchmark with no verdict-task variant, (b) CrossCodeEval already serves as our cross-file generation baseline, and (c) our study's contribution centers on verdict tasks where RepoBench offers no additional signal. Defects4J provides 2,274 labeled patches for APCA evaluation.
64	
65	Key gap: No prior work has (1) designed a trace representation specifically optimized for code behavior classification, or (2) systematically compared trace SFT effectiveness across verdict-classification-generation task spectrum with quantitative calibration analysis. DCSH covers generation only. TracePile scales trace SFT but evaluates only generation. TRACED shows traces help classification via pre-training encoders, but doesn't test decoder SFT on verdict tasks. LLM4PatchCorrect uses traces for APCA via ICL, not SFT. We fill all three gaps simultaneously.
66	
67	## Proposed Approach
68	
69	We propose Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction (VOTA), a novel execution trace representation designed specifically for code behavior classification, and conduct a systematic empirical study demonstrating when and why trace SFT helps across the verdict–prediction–generation task spectrum.
70	
71	**Method Contribution: VOTA Trace Representation.** Existing trace formats (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise from DCSH; CoE from TracePile) are designed for full execution simulation — capturing every variable state, every loop iteration, every line of execution. This is appropriate for generation tasks that require exact output prediction, but excessive for verdict tasks where the model only needs to determine whether code behaves correctly. VOTA is designed around the principle that verdict tasks require only decision-relevant execution states:
72	• Assertion-point variable snapshots: Capture variable states only at test assertion points and function entry/exit boundaries, not at every line. For a test with 5 assertions, this yields ~5 state snapshots vs. potentially hundreds for full-trace formats.
73	• Exception summaries: Type + message + triggering line only, not full stack traces. Captures the diagnostic signal while discarding syntactic noise.
74	• Loop compression: First iteration state, last iteration state, iteration count, and any iteration where state diverges from the pattern. This directly addresses the token-budget exhaustion failure mode identified by Debugging CWM (arXiv 2602.07672).
75	• Collection boundaries: For lists/dicts/sets, capture size + first/last elements + any elements referenced in assertions, not full contents.
76	• Behavioral delta format: For patch correctness tasks, VOTA additionally captures a behavioral diff — how the patched code's execution states differ from the original at assertion points — directly encoding the information most relevant to the correct/overfitting verdict.
77	
78	The design is motivated by an information-theoretic argument: verdict tasks have O(1) output entropy (1 bit for binary, log₂k bits for k-way classification), so the trace should contain only the information needed to determine that output, not the full O(n) execution simulation. We systematically ablate VOTA against all 5 DCSH trace representations (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise) on each task type to validate this design.
79	
80	**Task Taxonomy.** We define three categories by output space constraint: (1) Verdict tasks — binary/categorical judgments: patch correctness (correct/overfitting), test outcome prediction (pass/fail), bug detection (buggy/clean). (2) Constrained prediction — generating specific values: CRUXEval-O, LiveCodeBench test output prediction. (3) Open generation — producing arbitrary code: HumanEval, MBPP, CrossCodeEval. Our hypothesis: VOTA provides maximal benefit for verdict tasks, moderate benefit for constrained prediction, and no benefit (or harm) for generation — and this gradient is explained by calibration dynamics.
81	
82	**Data Construction & Trace Collection (~35h wall-clock, CPU-bound, parallelizable).**
83	• APCA-Defects4J: 2,274 labeled patches (1,169 correct, 1,105 overfitting). Apply each patch, run relevant tests (~10–20/patch) with JUnit instrumentation capturing variable states at assertion points, exception types, and loop counts. Generate both VOTA format (assertion-point snapshots + behavioral deltas) and SemCoder-style full NL monologues (for controlled comparison). Augment with PraPatch (1,988 patches). ~30h wall-clock on 4-core machine.
84	• TestVerdict-HumanEval/MBPP: Generate 10 solutions per problem using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (mix of correct and incorrect). Run each against test cases with Python sys.settrace instrumentation. ~664 problems × 10 solutions = ~6,640 (solution, test, trace, pass/fail) examples. ~3h wall-clock.
85	• BugDetect-DebugBench: Take 4,253 buggy programs + their correct versions. Run both on LeetCode test cases with trace instrumentation. ~8,500 (program, trace, buggy/clean + bug_type) examples. ~2h wall-clock.
86	• CRUXEval traces: 800 Python functions, instrument execution with sys.settrace. ~1h wall-clock.
87	
88	**Trace Abstraction (GPU, ~20–25h H100).** Convert raw traces to six formats for systematic comparison:
89	(1) VOTA (our proposed format): assertion-point snapshots + exception summaries + loop compression + collection boundaries + behavioral deltas.
90	(2–6) Five DCSH formats reproduced: Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise — using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for NL conversion following DCSH methodology.
91	This six-way comparison is the core ablation that validates VOTA as a novel trace representation.
92	
93	**Trace-Supervised SFT (GPU, ~80–90h H100).** Fine-tune two base models with LoRA (rank 32, alpha 64):
94	• Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (primary, strong code model)
95	• DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct (for direct comparison with DCSH which used this model)
96	
97	Training format by task type:
98	• Verdict tasks: input = (code + test + instruction) → output = (trace reasoning in [VOTA | comparison format] + verdict label). The model learns to generate execution-grounded chain-of-thought before predicting the verdict.
99	• CRUXEval-O: input = (function + input value) → output = (trace reasoning + predicted output). Matches DCSH protocol.
100	• Generation tasks: standard SFT without trace supervision (replication of DCSH setup).
101	
102	Training configurations: For each of the 2 models × 6 trace formats × 3 verdict tasks = 36 verdict-task runs, plus 2 models × 6 formats × 2 constrained-prediction tasks = 24 constrained-prediction runs, plus 2 models × 3 generation baselines = 6 generation runs. Total: 66 training runs. We train separate LoRA adapters per configuration to isolate effects, plus a multi-task VOTA model trained on all verdict tasks jointly.
103	
104	**Go/No-Go Pilot (GPU, ~8h H100).** Before committing full resources, we run a rapid pilot: train on 20% of APCA-Defects4J data with VOTA vs. SemCoder vs. no-trace baseline, evaluate on held-out fold. Decision criteria: (a) If VOTA shows ≥2% improvement over no-trace and ≥1% over SemCoder, proceed with full experiments in positive-result framing; (b) If trace SFT shows no improvement for verdicts, shift to negative-result framing with emphasis on calibration analysis explaining WHY.
105	
106	**Evaluation Protocol.**
107	• Verdict tasks: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples). McNemar's test for pairwise comparison with baselines. For APCA: 5-fold cross-validation matching ComPass's protocol.
108	• CRUXEval-O: pass@1, matching DCSH protocol exactly.
109	• LiveCodeBench test output prediction: pass@1 on problems after model training cutoff.
110	• Generation tasks (HumanEval, MBPP, CrossCodeEval): pass@1 / exact match / edit similarity, replicating DCSH.
111	
112	**Core Analyses — Five Primary Contributions.**
113	
114	(1) VOTA Trace Format Ablation (METHOD contribution): Systematic comparison of VOTA against all 5 DCSH trace representations on each task type. We measure: (a) accuracy/pass@1 per format per task, (b) token efficiency (average trace length in tokens), (c) accuracy-per-token metric showing VOTA achieves better accuracy with fewer tokens for verdict tasks. If VOTA outperforms full-simulation formats on verdict tasks while using 3–5× fewer tokens, this validates the design principle that verdict tasks need decision-relevant states, not full simulation.
115	
116	(2) Quantitative Calibration Analysis (FINDING contribution): We operationalize the DCSH overconfidence observation with rigorous calibration metrics. For each model × trace format × task configuration, we measure: (a) Expected Calibration Error (ECE) with 15 equal-width bins, following Spiess et al. (ICSE 2025) methodology; (b) Brier score decomposition (reliability + resolution + uncertainty) to isolate whether trace SFT improves discrimination or just shifts confidence; (c) reliability diagrams plotting observed accuracy vs. predicted confidence, comparing trace-SFT vs. no-trace models on verdict tasks and generation tasks; (d) confidence distribution histograms showing how trace SFT reshapes the prediction confidence landscape. The testable prediction: trace SFT decreases ECE for verdict tasks (sharpens decision boundaries → better calibration for binary outcomes) while increasing ECE for generation tasks (overconfident wrong predictions). If confirmed, this provides a mechanistic explanation for the DCSH finding and identifies the task-regime boundary.
117	
118	(3) Task-Spectrum Analysis (EMPIRICAL contribution): Plot trace SFT improvement (Δ accuracy/pass@1) vs. output space constraint across all tasks, using both VOTA and the best DCSH format. Test the hypothesis that benefit monotonically decreases as output space expands: verdict > constrained prediction > generation.
119	
120	(4) APCA Ensemble — Breaking the 88% Plateau (PRACTICAL contribution): Error-type analysis showing VOTA-SFT catches behaviorally incorrect patches (execution divergence at assertion points) that static methods (ComPass, Historian) miss, and vice versa. Concrete ensemble configurations: (a) majority vote (VOTA-SFT + ComPass + Historian), (b) learned stacking (logistic regression on the three models' predictions), (c) confidence-weighted ensemble using calibrated probabilities from (2). Target: >90% accuracy on Defects4J, breaking the ~88% plateau. This is positioned as a primary headline result: behavioral + static complementarity yields practical APCA improvement.
121	
122	(5) SFT Internalization vs. ICL (EFFICIENCY contribution): Head-to-head with LLM4PatchCorrect showing our SFT internalization achieves competitive or better accuracy while requiring no traces at inference time. We measure inference-time speedup (no trace collection overhead) and accuracy comparison.
123	
124	**Additional Ablations:** (a) LoRA rank (16/32/64), (b) training data size curves (10%/20%/50%/100%), (c) VOTA component ablation (remove each component: assertion-point snapshots, loop compression, behavioral deltas) to validate

## Core Problem

"Do Code Semantics Help?" (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.11686) concluded that execution trace-based SFT provides limited benefit for Code LLMs, finding it fails to improve code synthesis in 7/9 configurations and yields inconsistent results for CRUXEval reasoning tasks. TracePile (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2510.23629) scaled trace SFT to 2.6M samples across four base models and 20 benchmarks, achieving strong gains on math and code reasoning — but evaluated only generative tasks. Across all existing trace SFT studies, every task requires generating exact outputs: complete programs, precise I/O values, repaired code, or mathematical derivations. We ask: does trace SFT help for code behavior verdict tasks — binary/categorical predictions about execution outcomes (pass/fail, correct/incorrect, buggy/clean) — where the output space is fundamentally constrained? Moreover, can a trace representation specifically designed for classification (capturing only decision-relevant execution states) outperform trace formats designed for full execution simulation? This distinction — verdict prediction with task-optimized trace representation vs. open generation with simulation-oriented traces — has not been systematically investigated.

## Opportunity / Why Now

Four converging lines of evidence suggest trace SFT may differentially benefit verdict tasks over generation, and that a task-optimized trace representation can amplify this benefit. First, SemCoder (NeurIPS 2024) demonstrates that trace-supervised training teaches genuine behavioral understanding (63.6% CRUXEval-I vs. 50.3% for Code Llama 34B). Second, TracePile (NeurIPS 2025) shows that even at 2.6M-sample scale, trace SFT has only been applied to generative tasks — the classification regime is entirely untested. Third, TRACED (ICSE 2024) provides a precedent from the pre-training paradigm: execution-aware pre-training significantly improves encoder-model performance on classification tasks (vulnerability detection, clone retrieval), suggesting that execution understanding transfers to classification — but nobody has tested this for decoder SFT. Fourth, "Debugging Code World Models" (arXiv 2602.07672) identifies token-budget exhaustion as a dominant failure mode in dense trace representations, motivating our design of a compact, verdict-focused trace format.

The practical stakes are high: automated patch correctness assessment (APCA) plateaus at ~88% accuracy (ComPass: 88.35%, Historian: 88.4%) using purely static features, test outcome prediction is increasingly critical for efficient CI/CD, and bug detection accuracy determines triage quality. An ensemble combining trace-SFT behavioral analysis with static approaches could break the 90% APCA barrier — a concrete practical headline. The study design ensures publishable value regardless of outcome: if our Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction (VOTA) helps for verdict tasks, we contribute both a novel trace representation and a new task regime where code semantics help; if it doesn't, we strengthen and extend the DCSH negative finding with quantitative calibration analysis explaining WHY traces fail across the full task spectrum.

## Landscape (SOTA & Limitations)

Trace SFT for Code LLMs: "Do Code Semantics Help?" (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.11686) is the central prior work. Testing five trace representations (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise) across DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, and Gemma2-9B, they found trace SFT fails for code synthesis (7/9 configs), yields marginal gains for program repair (+0.3–1.4 pts with SemCoder only), and shows inconsistent CRUXEval results. Crucially, all their tasks are generative — no verdict/classification tasks were evaluated, and their trace representations were designed for execution simulation, not classification. TracePile (arXiv 2510.23629, NeurIPS 2025) represents the largest-scale trace SFT effort: 2.6M Chain of Execution (CoE) samples across LLaMA 3, LLaMA 3.1, Qwen-2.5, and Qwen-2.5 Coder, evaluated on 20 benchmarks covering math, code, logic, and algorithms. It achieves strong gains (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B CRUXEval: 23.5% → 49.4%) but exclusively targets generative tasks — verdict/classification tasks are absent from their evaluation, reinforcing our gap. SemCoder (arXiv 2406.01006, NeurIPS 2024) trains on monologue-style NL execution descriptions and achieves strong CRUXEval gains, showing trace training CAN teach behavioral understanding. Execution Tuning (E.T., arXiv 2503.05703, 2025) achieves ~80% on CRUXEval-O with dynamic scratchpads but requires traces at inference time — we aim to internalize this capability via SFT. ExecVerify (arXiv 2603.11226, 2026) uses white-box RL rewards from execution traces, enabling 7B ≈ 32B on reasoning benchmarks. "Code Execution as Grounded Supervision" (arXiv 2506.10343, EMNLP 2025) extracts verifiable CoT from code execution for general reasoning. Self-Execution Simulation (arXiv 2604.03253, 2026) trains on NL traces + RL for competitive programming self-verification (+5.5% via best-of-k).

Execution Traces for Code Classification (Pre-training Paradigm): TRACED (arXiv 2306.07487, ICSE 2024) is an important precedent: it pre-trains code language models with source code, executable inputs, and execution traces, then fine-tunes on downstream classification tasks including vulnerability detection and clone retrieval, significantly outperforming statically pre-trained models. This demonstrates that execution understanding transfers to classification. However, TRACED uses encoder-based pre-training (not decoder SFT), operates at the pre-training stage (not task-specific SFT), and does not test on verdict tasks (pass/fail, patch correctness). Our work extends this insight to the decoder SFT paradigm and tests it systematically on code behavior verdict tasks.

Correctness Signals in Code SFT: FGIT (arXiv 2503.16913, ASE 2025) uses correct/incorrect code signal during SFT with dynamic loss weighting on error-sensitive segments, achieving 6.9% relative improvement on pass@1 for code generation. While technically different (loss reweighting for generation, not trace-supervised classification), it occupies a conceptually adjacent space: leveraging fault information to improve code SFT. Our approach differs in both objective (classification vs. generation) and mechanism (trace-grounded reasoning vs. loss reweighting).

Automated Patch Correctness Assessment (APCA): ComPass (arXiv 2602.07561, 2026) achieves 88.35% accuracy on Defects4J via contrastive learning on BERT representations — purely static. Historian (arXiv 2603.00649, 2026) achieves 88.4% accuracy with 95.0% coverage by comparing patches against historically validated fixes — also static. APSG/Graph-LoRA (arXiv 2505.02629, 2025) reaches 85.8–96.8% via attributed semantic graphs + LLaMA3 fine-tuning. RePaCA (arXiv 2507.22580, 2025) uses reasoning LLMs with generic CoT at 83.1%. LLM4PatchCorrect (TSE 2024) is the closest existing work: it uses execution traces as in-context learning input for StarCoder, achieving 84.4% accuracy — but requires traces at inference time (expensive), while we internalize trace reasoning via SFT. Shibboleth (ISSTA 2022) achieves 88.7% but requires test execution at inference. APPT (TSE 2024) uses BERT+LSTM at 79.7%. No existing APCA method uses trace-supervised SFT with a verdict-optimized trace representation.

Calibration of Code LLMs: Spiess et al. (arXiv 2402.02047, ICSE 2025) establish the first calibration framework for code-generating models, finding they are poorly calibrated out-of-the-box and that Platt scaling helps. However, they study calibration only for generation tasks. "Do Code Semantics Help?" (Table 7) observed that trace SFT boosts prediction confidence without increasing correctness for generative tasks. We hypothesize this overconfidence effect is beneficial for classification (sharper decision boundaries) while harmful for generation (confidently wrong outputs), and we operationalize this with ECE, Brier score, and reliability diagrams — the first quantitative calibration analysis of trace SFT across the verdict-generation spectrum.

Benchmarks: CRUXEval (arXiv 2401.03065, ICML 2024) provides 800 Python functions for execution prediction. LiveCodeBench (arXiv 2403.07974) offers contamination-free code evaluation. DebugBench (2024) has 4,253 instances across C++/Java/Python with 18 bug types. CrossCodeEval (arXiv 2310.11248, NeurIPS 2023) evaluates cross-file code completion across 4 languages. RepoBench (arXiv 2306.03091, ICLR 2024) evaluates repository-level code completion; we exclude it because (a) it is a generation benchmark with no verdict-task variant, (b) CrossCodeEval already serves as our cross-file generation baseline, and (c) our study's contribution centers on verdict tasks where RepoBench offers no additional signal. Defects4J provides 2,274 labeled patches for APCA evaluation.

Key gap: No prior work has (1) designed a trace representation specifically optimized for code behavior classification, or (2) systematically compared trace SFT effectiveness across verdict-classification-generation task spectrum with quantitative calibration analysis. DCSH covers generation only. TracePile scales trace SFT but evaluates only generation. TRACED shows traces help classification via pre-training encoders, but doesn't test decoder SFT on verdict tasks. LLM4PatchCorrect uses traces for APCA via ICL, not SFT. We fill all three gaps simultaneously.

## Proposed Approach

We propose Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction (VOTA), a novel execution trace representation designed specifically for code behavior classification, and conduct a systematic empirical study demonstrating when and why trace SFT helps across the verdict–prediction–generation task spectrum.

**Method Contribution: VOTA Trace Representation.** Existing trace formats (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise from DCSH; CoE from TracePile) are designed for full execution simulation — capturing every variable state, every loop iteration, every line of execution. This is appropriate for generation tasks that require exact output prediction, but excessive for verdict tasks where the model only needs to determine whether code behaves correctly. VOTA is designed around the principle that verdict tasks require only decision-relevant execution states:
• Assertion-point variable snapshots: Capture variable states only at test assertion points and function entry/exit boundaries, not at every line. For a test with 5 assertions, this yields ~5 state snapshots vs. potentially hundreds for full-trace formats.
• Exception summaries: Type + message + triggering line only, not full stack traces. Captures the diagnostic signal while discarding syntactic noise.
• Loop compression: First iteration state, last iteration state, iteration count, and any iteration where state diverges from the pattern. This directly addresses the token-budget exhaustion failure mode identified by Debugging CWM (arXiv 2602.07672).
• Collection boundaries: For lists/dicts/sets, capture size + first/last elements + any elements referenced in assertions, not full contents.
• Behavioral delta format: For patch correctness tasks, VOTA additionally captures a behavioral diff — how the patched code's execution states differ from the original at assertion points — directly encoding the information most relevant to the correct/overfitting verdict.

The design is motivated by an information-theoretic argument: verdict tasks have O(1) output entropy (1 bit for binary, log₂k bits for k-way classification), so the trace should contain only the information needed to determine that output, not the full O(n) execution simulation. We systematically ablate VOTA against all 5 DCSH trace representations (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise) on each task type to validate this design.

**Task Taxonomy.** We define three categories by output space constraint: (1) Verdict tasks — binary/categorical judgments: patch correctness (correct/overfitting), test outcome prediction (pass/fail), bug detection (buggy/clean). (2) Constrained prediction — generating specific values: CRUXEval-O, LiveCodeBench test output prediction. (3) Open generation — producing arbitrary code: HumanEval, MBPP, CrossCodeEval. Our hypothesis: VOTA provides maximal benefit for verdict tasks, moderate benefit for constrained prediction, and no benefit (or harm) for generation — and this gradient is explained by calibration dynamics.

**Data Construction & Trace Collection (~35h wall-clock, CPU-bound, parallelizable).**
• APCA-Defects4J: 2,274 labeled patches (1,169 correct, 1,105 overfitting). Apply each patch, run relevant tests (~10–20/patch) with JUnit instrumentation capturing variable states at assertion points, exception types, and loop counts. Generate both VOTA format (assertion-point snapshots + behavioral deltas) and SemCoder-style full NL monologues (for controlled comparison). Augment with PraPatch (1,988 patches). ~30h wall-clock on 4-core machine.
• TestVerdict-HumanEval/MBPP: Generate 10 solutions per problem using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (mix of correct and incorrect). Run each against test cases with Python sys.settrace instrumentation. ~664 problems × 10 solutions = ~6,640 (solution, test, trace, pass/fail) examples. ~3h wall-clock.
• BugDetect-DebugBench: Take 4,253 buggy programs + their correct versions. Run both on LeetCode test cases with trace instrumentation. ~8,500 (program, trace, buggy/clean + bug_type) examples. ~2h wall-clock.
• CRUXEval traces: 800 Python functions, instrument execution with sys.settrace. ~1h wall-clock.

**Trace Abstraction (GPU, ~20–25h H100).** Convert raw traces to six formats for systematic comparison:
(1) VOTA (our proposed format): assertion-point snapshots + exception summaries + loop compression + collection boundaries + behavioral deltas.
(2–6) Five DCSH formats reproduced: Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise — using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for NL conversion following DCSH methodology.
This six-way comparison is the core ablation that validates VOTA as a novel trace representation.

**Trace-Supervised SFT (GPU, ~80–90h H100).** Fine-tune two base models with LoRA (rank 32, alpha 64):
• Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (primary, strong code model)
• DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct (for direct comparison with DCSH which used this model)

Training format by task type:
• Verdict tasks: input = (code + test + instruction) → output = (trace reasoning in [VOTA | comparison format] + verdict label). The model learns to generate execution-grounded chain-of-thought before predicting the verdict.
• CRUXEval-O: input = (function + input value) → output = (trace reasoning + predicted output). Matches DCSH protocol.
• Generation tasks: standard SFT without trace supervision (replication of DCSH setup).

Training configurations: For each of the 2 models × 6 trace formats × 3 verdict tasks = 36 verdict-task runs, plus 2 models × 6 formats × 2 constrained-prediction tasks = 24 constrained-prediction runs, plus 2 models × 3 generation baselines = 6 generation runs. Total: 66 training runs. We train separate LoRA adapters per configuration to isolate effects, plus a multi-task VOTA model trained on all verdict tasks jointly.

**Go/No-Go Pilot (GPU, ~8h H100).** Before committing full resources, we run a rapid pilot: train on 20% of APCA-Defects4J data with VOTA vs. SemCoder vs. no-trace baseline, evaluate on held-out fold. Decision criteria: (a) If VOTA shows ≥2% improvement over no-trace and ≥1% over SemCoder, proceed with full experiments in positive-result framing; (b) If trace SFT shows no improvement for verdicts, shift to negative-result framing with emphasis on calibration analysis explaining WHY.

**Evaluation Protocol.**
• Verdict tasks: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples). McNemar's test for pairwise comparison with baselines. For APCA: 5-fold cross-validation matching ComPass's protocol.
• CRUXEval-O: pass@1, matching DCSH protocol exactly.
• LiveCodeBench test output prediction: pass@1 on problems after model training cutoff.
• Generation tasks (HumanEval, MBPP, CrossCodeEval): pass@1 / exact match / edit similarity, replicating DCSH.

**Core Analyses — Five Primary Contributions.**

(1) VOTA Trace Format Ablation (METHOD contribution): Systematic comparison of VOTA against all 5 DCSH trace representations on each task type. We measure: (a) accuracy/pass@1 per format per task, (b) token efficiency (average trace length in tokens), (c) accuracy-per-token metric showing VOTA achieves better accuracy with fewer tokens for verdict tasks. If VOTA outperforms full-simulation formats on verdict tasks while using 3–5× fewer tokens, this validates the design principle that verdict tasks need decision-relevant states, not full simulation.

(2) Quantitative Calibration Analysis (FINDING contribution): We operationalize the DCSH overconfidence observation with rigorous calibration metrics. For each model × trace format × task configuration, we measure: (a) Expected Calibration Error (ECE) with 15 equal-width bins, following Spiess et al. (ICSE 2025) methodology; (b) Brier score decomposition (reliability + resolution + uncertainty) to isolate whether trace SFT improves discrimination or just shifts confidence; (c) reliability diagrams plotting observed accuracy vs. predicted confidence, comparing trace-SFT vs. no-trace models on verdict tasks and generation tasks; (d) confidence distribution histograms showing how trace SFT reshapes the prediction confidence landscape. The testable prediction: trace SFT decreases ECE for verdict tasks (sharpens decision boundaries → better calibration for binary outcomes) while increasing ECE for generation tasks (overconfident wrong predictions). If confirmed, this provides a mechanistic explanation for the DCSH finding and identifies the task-regime boundary.

(3) Task-Spectrum Analysis (EMPIRICAL contribution): Plot trace SFT improvement (Δ accuracy/pass@1) vs. output space constraint across all tasks, using both VOTA and the best DCSH format. Test the hypothesis that benefit monotonically decreases as output space expands: verdict > constrained prediction > generation.

(4) APCA Ensemble — Breaking the 88% Plateau (PRACTICAL contribution): Error-type analysis showing VOTA-SFT catches behaviorally incorrect patches (execution divergence at assertion points) that static methods (ComPass, Historian) miss, and vice versa. Concrete ensemble configurations: (a) majority vote (VOTA-SFT + ComPass + Historian), (b) learned stacking (logistic regression on the three models' predictions), (c) confidence-weighted ensemble using calibrated probabilities from (2). Target: >90% accuracy on Defects4J, breaking the ~88% plateau. This is positioned as a primary headline result: behavioral + static complementarity yields practical APCA improvement.

(5) SFT Internalization vs. ICL (EFFICIENCY contribution): Head-to-head with LLM4PatchCorrect showing our SFT internalization achieves competitive or better accuracy while requiring no traces at inference time. We measure inference-time speedup (no trace collection overhead) and accuracy comparison.

2	
3	Execution traces record a program's complete runtime behavior: every function call, variable assignment, and control flow decision.

8	
9	Verdict prediction offers a clean testbed for isolating this effect.
10	As binary classification, it separates signal extraction from generation noise; as fault detection, the model need only detect failure, not simulate execution.
11	If the fault signal concentrates in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
12	Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation tasks where this density hypothesis could not be cleanly tested.
13

17

20	Gradient masking bounds the backward-pass contribution to ${\sim}$4pp (\S\ref{sec:density}), a tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}), and cross-dataset transfer to DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the component ranking (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).

23	\begin{enumerate}
24	\item \textbf{Information density as the binding constraint on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learning}: training dynamics, gradient masking (${\sim}$4pp backward-pass contribution), and cross-model convergence confirm that compact trace inputs learn faster and more stably than verbose ones, independent of model scale (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:density}).

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces record a program's complete runtime behavior: every function call, variable assignment, and control flow decision.
Recent work has incorporated them into code language models for tasks from bug localization to program repair \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}, under the working assumption that richer runtime information yields better predictions.
\emph{We find the opposite.}
For verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), feeding a model the complete execution trace produces accuracies of 79--82\%, barely above a source-code-only baseline (72--76\%), while a single compact component of the same trace reaches ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models tested.
Verbose traces do not just fail to help; they actively impair learning.

Verdict prediction offers a clean testbed for isolating this effect.
As binary classification, it separates signal extraction from generation noise; as fault detection, the model need only detect failure, not simulate execution.
If the fault signal concentrates in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation tasks where this density hypothesis could not be cleanly tested.

We conduct the first systematic component ablation of trace representations, decomposing Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction (VOTA; exception events + assertion comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families \citep{qwen2025coder,roziere2024code,deepseek2024coder}, on 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}.
The results are unambiguous: exception events (a median of 150 tokens encoding error type, stack frame, and message) reach ${\geq}$99.33\% accuracy across all models and seeds, converging within 50 training steps.
Full traces plateau near 82\% and gradient-masked variants reach only ${\sim}$86\%, both without stable convergence. This confirms that information density, not model capacity, is the binding constraint (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).

This finding is robust to several potential confounds.
Removing format markers preserves accuracy within 2pp, and on 8 boundary samples where exceptions appear in passing code, the fine-tuned model correctly classifies 6/8 vs.\ 0/8 for a regex baseline, which confirms the signal is semantic (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).
Gradient masking bounds the backward-pass contribution to ${\sim}$4pp (\S\ref{sec:density}), a tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}), and cross-dataset transfer to DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the component ranking (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Information density as the binding constraint on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learning}: training dynamics, gradient masking (${\sim}$4pp backward-pass contribution), and cross-model convergence confirm that compact trace inputs learn faster and more stably than verbose ones, independent of model scale (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:density}).
\item \textbf{Exception events as the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models with zero cross-seed variance on Qwen and sub-1pp cross-model range (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
\item \textbf{A two-tier diagnostic hierarchy with quantitative decomposition}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertion comparisons) are individually sufficient for near-perfect accuracy and generalize across architectures within a 0.50--1.11pp cross-model range, while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) are model-dependent with ${\sim}$9pp range; a sharp phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens spatially localizes the diagnostic boundary (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy by trace condition (Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B vs.\ DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, $N{=}1{,}190$). \cond{exception\_only} shows near-identical accuracy across models ($\Delta{=}0.5$pp), while \cond{VOTA} exhibits a 15pp cross-model gap due to a tokenizer-induced training failure (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).}
\label{fig:cross_scale}
\end{figure}

\section{Method}

\subsection{Task Definition}

We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.
The model produces a single token (\textit{pass} or \textit{fail}), making this a binary classification task.
Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution.
The discrete binary outcome makes the effect of each trace component directly measurable, providing cleaner ablation contrasts than generation tasks where output quality varies continuously.

\subsection{Dataset}
\label{sec:dataset}

We sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \textit{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\% pass, 33\% fail).
The dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\%).
The \cond{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\% train, 48.99\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).

\subsection{Trace Representations}

We define seven conditions that vary the trace information available:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=1em]
\item \cond{no\_trace}: source code and test input only.
\item \cond{full\_trace}: complete line-by-line trace with variable states.
\item \cond{VOTA}: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).
\item \cond{exception\_only}: exception and error events only.
\item \cond{ae\_only}: assertion-point actual/expected pairs only.
\item \cond{loop\_only}: loop compression summaries only.
\item \cond{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Models and Training}

We evaluate four models spanning three architecture families: \textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct} \citep{qwen2025coder}, \textbf{CodeLlama-13B-Instruct} \citep{roziere2024code}, and \textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \citep{deepseek2024coder}, covering a 1.5B--13B parameter range (8.7$\times$).

Sequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.
The primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \cond{exception\_only} robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_details}).

\subsection{Loss Ablation}

To disentangle training signal from input signal quality, we introduce \cond{full\_trace\_label\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).
Improvement over standard \cond{full\_trace} is attributable to backward-pass signal dilution; the remaining gap to VOTA reflects inference-time input complexity.
